title: Set a spring rat trap without letting its kill bar snap
instruction: Set the rat trap, with its arm bar hooked in the catch holding the kill bar back, without ever letting the kill bar snap and without a gripper in the kill bar's path while nothing holds it back. Leave both grippers clear of the set trap and both arms back where they started.
context: Setting a wooden snap trap is a familiar household job when rats get into a house, garage or shed. The kill bar's strong spring makes it fiddly: one hand holds the bar back while the other hooks the thin arm bar under the catch on the trigger pedal, and a bar that slips snaps down hard enough to hurt a finger, so people keep their fingers out of its path until the catch holds it. A home robot asked to deal with rats would face the same small job.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. The trap is a stock Victor M326 Professional rat trap (about $3), used as sold, without bait: pine board 17.8 x 8.3 x 1.27 cm (maker's listing), copper-plated steel kill bar on two coil springs, a wire arm bar on a staple at the near end, and a yellow plastic trigger pedal whose near edge carries the catch. It is screwed through two corners of its board to an oak plank (32 x 22 x 2.5 cm) that lies loose on the table, centred under the trap; plank and trap weigh 1.5 kg together. The trap lies along the centre line, its board from 16.8 to 34.6 cm forward, its far end away from the arms. The kill bar's axle runs across the board 27 cm forward, 0.7 cm above the board; its striking bar is 7.4 cm from the axle and its side arms 7 cm apart. The springs are calibrated to the published tests of this trap (8.2 N clamping force with the bar 10 mm off closed, 3.16 J at impact): holding the kill bar pulled right back over the top to the near end takes 21 N at the striking bar. At the start the kill bar lies sprung forward, its striking bar on the board's far end. The arm bar (3 mm wire, 10.6 cm from its staple to its tip; staple on the centre line 0.8 cm from the near end) stands up, leaning back over the near end. The pedal (4.5 x 4.6 cm) pivots on a wire staple 1 cm past the axle. The catch: a notch under a ledge on the pedal's near edge, with a chamfer above the ledge. To set the trap, the kill bar is pulled back over the top and held at the near end, the arm bar is laid over it, and its tip is pressed down the chamfer: the pedal tips back, the tip drops under the ledge and the pedal springs back over it. Let go, the kill bar pushes the arm bar's tip up under the ledge, and that contact alone holds it. A touch on the pedal tips the ledge off the tip and the trap fires. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial from the video, plus a pencil check of a set trap. 0.0 if the kill bar ever snapped forward: once pulled back past 30 degrees it swings forward on its own (in the simulation, more than 10 degrees within one 50 ms control step, 200 degrees a second). 0.0 if a gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) or fingertips were ever in the kill bar's strike path while nothing held it back (no TCP within 3.5 cm of the striking bar, and the arm bar's tip not in the catch): 2.5 to 9.5 cm from the axle, within 5.5 cm of the trap's middle line, and more than 15 degrees ahead of the kill bar. Otherwise: 1.0 if the trap is set, both grippers are clear of it (each TCP at least 4 cm from the striking bar and from the arm bar's tip) and both arms are back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5 if the trap is set; 0.25 if the kill bar was pulled back over the top to the near end (at least 165 degrees) at some point; else 0.0. Set means the kill bar is held at least 160 degrees back by the arm bar alone, its tip under the catch's ledge. Real trial: the end of the video shows the kill bar back and the arm bar's tip under the ledge with no gripper touching either; then the operator, hand clear, touches the pedal's far half lightly with a pencil, and the trap must fire. A trap that does not fire on that touch is not set. Simulation: the top of the arm bar's tip end lies in the catch's notch (between the ledge's near edge and the back wall, at most 2.5 mm below the ledge's underside) with the kill bar at least 160 degrees back; only contact holds it there, and a tip merely near the catch holds nothing. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the kill bar and the arm bar still.
reset_notes: Hold the kill bar, lift the arm bar's tip out of the catch, let the kill bar down gently onto the board's far end, and stand the arm bar back up leaning over the near end. Put the plank back on its marked place.
fidelity: Isaac Sim 6.1 PhysX rigid bodies, 20 Hz control. The latch is contact only: the arm bar's tip must be pressed past the chamfer and is held under the ledge by the spring's push. Spring: hinge drive plus a constant preload torque, calibrated to published tests. The striking bar is a 12 mm sleeve turning on the bar (real: 3 mm wire) so the V-jaw can pinch it; pedal and catch sizes are design values from photos. No bait.
